children: By Staff Writer
NIGERIA’S agriculture sector contributes over 22 percent to Gross Domestic Product (GDP), but accounts for only 4.1 percent of merchandise exports.

This disparity was highlighted by stakeholders at the fifth FirstBank Agric & Export Expo, in Lagos on Wednesday, who attributed the issue to short-term financing, raw commodity exports, and weak value chains.

During the opening ceremony of the expo, key industry leaders emphasised that traditional short-term commercial loans are inadequate for agricultural financing. They stressed the importance of aligning credit structures with planting, harvest, and processing cycles to make farming globally competitive.

Lagos State governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu, represented by the Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Systems, Ruth Olusanya, stated that unlocking the nation’s economic potential requires financial institutions to adapt to the specific operational realities of agribusinesses.
“A good harvest without financing cannot become a good business, and a good product without market access cannot become a successful export.

“Our financing structures must recognise the realities of agriculture, including planting and harvest cycles, rather than imposing conventional short-term financing models on long-term agricultural businesses. Institutions like FirstBank can make a transformative difference in this area,” Sanwo-Olu explained.
He urged financial institutions and agro-processors to prioritise local value addition, warning that raw commodity exports limit economic prosperity.

“If you export raw products, you remain perpetually broke. By adding value, you can determine the global price. For example, cassava should not leave Nigeria as just cassava, and cocoa should not be exported as raw beans,” Sanwo-Olu added.

Reaffirming the bank’s commitment to supporting the sector, Chief Executive Officer of FirstBank Group, Olusegun Alebiosu, stated that the bank is shifting its focus from high-level discussions to targeted execution and capital deployment.

“Our objective is not only to showcase opportunities within agriculture and exports but also to facilitate connections, partnerships, financing solutions, market access opportunities, and knowledge exchange required to transform ideas into thriving enterprises.
“Over the years, this Expo has evolved into a leading platform for discussions and collaborations to advance Nigeria’s agricultural and non-oil export sectors,” Alebiosu said.

From a macroeconomic perspective, FirstBank Chief Economist Chinwe Egwim noted that although agriculture contributes over 20 percent to Nigeria’s Gross Domestic Product, it generates only 4.1 percent of total merchandise export earnings.

“When a sector contributes as much as 20 percent to total GDP but only 4.1 percent to merchandise trade, it reveals significant growth opportunities. Capital becomes more impactful when it connects these opportunities rather than treating each part of the value chain in isolation. Financing additional production yields greater commercial benefits when there is enough capacity for aggregation, storage, or processing of that output,” Egwim stated.

She advised agricultural exporters to adopt a market-led strategy rather than a commodity-first approach, designing products according to international buyer specifications, certification needs, and supply reliability.

Ronaldo Vieira, the Consul-General of Brazil in Lagos, shared insights from Brazil’s two-century agricultural transformation, mentioning that sustainable agro-export expansion relies on integrated collaboration between public policy, research entities, private finance, and farmers.

In their remarks, Ondo State Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa and Niger State Governor Mohammed Umaru Bago called for a stronger focus on agricultural value chains, food production, and export-oriented investments, as Nigeria faces challenges related to food imports, insecurity, and limited processing capacity.
They outlined agricultural investment opportunities in their respective states and urged financial institutions and the private sector to extend their focus beyond financing primary production.

Aiyedatiwa emphasised that Ondo State’s agricultural potential in cocoa, oil palm, cassava, fisheries, aquaculture, and livestock would only translate into prosperity if the government and the private sector develop the full value chains around these commodities.
“Comparative advantage alone does not create prosperity. Our responsibility as government is to convert that comparative advantage into competitive advantage,” Aiyedatiwa said.

He added that his administration is moving beyond primary production to focus on quality inputs, aggregation, processing, storage, logistics, traceability, standards, financing, and access to both domestic and international markets.
He noted that it is the government’s responsibility to develop agriculture in a holistic manner.

title: ZAWYA: Nigeria earns only four% of exports from agriculture despite 22% GDP share
